I am an economist and PhD candidate in the Department of Economics, Faculty of
Economics and Business, Universitas Indonesia, and a civil servant in the
Provincial Government of North Sulawesi. My work has two strands that are
usually kept apart: empirical research on how communities absorb large physical
shocks, and professional practice in Indonesian public procurement. They share a
single question: how public resources and collective capacity are actually
allocated when institutions are under strain.

My dissertation, *Shaking Land and Shaking Lives: Essays on the Economic Impacts
of Seismic Disasters*, asks what a damaging earthquake does to a village once
the rubble is cleared. The answer is not one-directional. Reported communal
conflict falls after damage-level shaking, while theft rises sharply on the same
villages in the same waves: not a general improvement in security, but a change
in the *kind* of violence a community can produce. Much of the work behind that
result is infrastructure rather than estimation, harmonising two decades of
village boundary change onto a constant reference year and turning seismic
intensity surfaces into village-level exposure. It is unglamorous, largely
unavailable off the shelf in Indonesia, and where most of the credibility of the
results comes from.

Before graduate school I entered the civil service through IPDN, and my early
posts in North Sulawesi were in asset management and procurement: procurement
officer, then commitment-making official responsible for contracts, then member
of the provincial selection working group, authorised to determine winning
providers for procurements up to IDR 100 billion. From 2021 to 2023 I led the
provincial sub-division responsible for procurement advisory and technical
guidance, and since 2018 I have worked nationally as a certified facilitator,
competency assessor, and advisor.

That practical experience shaped what I find worth studying. Procurement is
where formal rules meet local discretion, and where the gap between what a
regulation requires and what an official can actually do is most visible. My
master's thesis used Indonesia's e-procurement records to ask whether more
bidders produce better outcomes.

The longer-term agenda is to keep both strands running: rigorous empirical
economics on shocks, institutions, and local public goods in Indonesia, and a
serious contribution to the professionalisation of Indonesian public
procurement, including writing about procurement practice for practitioners,
not only for regulators.
